\(P\) on \(OM\): \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\lambda\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac\lambda2\underset{\sim}{a}+\lambda\underset{\sim}{c}\). \(P\) on \(AN\): \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\mu\overrightarrow{AN}=(1-\mu)\underset{\sim}{a}+\dfrac\mu2\underset{\sim}{c}\).
\(\underset{\sim}{a}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{c}\) are not parallel, so the coefficients match: \(\dfrac\lambda2=1-\mu\) and \(\lambda=\dfrac\mu2\).

questions.stem: Which parametric equations represent a circle?
questions.hint: A circle centred at the origin satisfies \(x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}\) with the same \(r\) for every \(t\). ELIMINATE the parameter \(t\) in each option.

steps.explain: A: \(t=\dfrac{x}{2}\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{x^{2}}{4}\), a PARABOLA. B: \(t=\dfrac{x}{2}\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{x}{2}+2\), a LINE.
C: \(\dfrac{x}{2}=\cos t\) and \(y=\sin t\), so \(\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^{2}+y^{2}=1\): an ELLIPSE (the \(x\)-radius is 2 but the \(y\)-radius is 1).
D: square and add. The cross terms \(\pm8\sin t\cos t\) cancel.
Answer: D.
So the correct choice is option D.

parts.stem: \(\Delta ADO\) and \(\Delta CFO\) are congruent triangles. By considering the lengths of \(AD\) and \(CF\), show that \(\left|\overrightarrow{WY}\right|=\left|\overrightarrow{WZ}\right|\).
parts.hint: AD = CF from the congruent triangles; WY and WZ are half of these.

From (i), each of \(WY\) and \(WZ\) is half of these.

parts.answer: Since △ADO ≅ △CFO, AD = CF. From (i), \(|\overrightarrow{WY}|=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AD}|\) and \(|\overrightarrow{WZ}|=\frac12|\overrightarrow{CF}|\), so \(|\overrightarrow{WY}|=|\overrightarrow{WZ}|\).

keyPoints.note: Use AD = CF and the halving result from (i).

parts.stem: Let \(\angle COD=\theta\) as shown above, show that \(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{f}=-\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{d}\).
parts.hint: ∠AOF = 180° − θ; use cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ and equal sides of the squares.

steps.explain: Angles at \(O\) add to \(360^\circ\). \(\angle AOC=\angle DOF=90^\circ\) (square corners).
Write \(\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OF}\) with the angle formula, using \(\cos(180^\circ-\theta)=-\cos\theta\).
Sides of a square are equal: \(|2\mathbf a|=|2\mathbf c|\) and \(|2\mathbf f|=|2\mathbf d|\).
Divide both sides by 4.

parts.answer: ∠AOC = ∠DOF = 90°, so ∠AOF = 360° − 90° − 90° − θ = 180° − θ. Then \(2\mathbf a\cdot2\mathbf f=|2\mathbf a||2\mathbf f|\cos(180°-\theta)=-|2\mathbf a||2\mathbf f|\cos\theta\). As |2a| = |2c| and |2f| = |2d| (sides of squares), this equals \(-|2\mathbf c||2\mathbf d|\cos\theta=-2\mathbf c\cdot2\mathbf d\). Dividing by 4: \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf f=-\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf d\).

keyPoints.note: Find ∠AOF in terms of θ, then compare OA·OF with OC·OD.

parts.stem: By considering the dot product of vectors \(\overrightarrow{WY}\) and \(\overrightarrow{WZ}\), as well as the results from parts (ii) and (iii), show that \(WYXZ\) is a square.
parts.hint: Expand (d − a)·(f − c), use (iii), and remember a·c = d·f = 0.

steps.explain: Use (i).
By (iii), \(-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf f=\mathbf c\cdot\mathbf d\), which cancels \(-\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf c\).
\(OD\perp OF\) and \(OA\perp OC\) (square corners), so both dot products are 0.
So \(WY\perp WZ\). With \(|WY|=|WZ|\) from (ii), the parallelogram \(WYXZ\) has a pair of equal, perpendicular adjacent sides, so it is a square.

steps.explain: Column form: \(\underset{\sim}{u}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\underset{\sim}{v}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Dot product: multiply matching components and add.
Magnitudes: \(|\underset{\sim}{u}|=\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt2\) and \(|\underset{\sim}{v}|=\sqrt{1+1}=\sqrt2\).

Substitute: \(\cos\theta=\dfrac{0}{\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2}=0\), so \(\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) (\(90^{\circ}\)). In the diagram \(\underset{\sim}{u}\) is at \(+45^{\circ}\) and \(\underset{\sim}{v}\) at \(-45^{\circ}\): the angle between them is \(45^{\circ}+45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}\).

Why not the others: \(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\) is the angle of each vector with the \(x\)-axis, not between them; \(\pi\) would mean opposite directions and \(2\pi\) is a full turn (not an angle between vectors).
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: Points \(A,B\) have position vectors \(\overrightarrow{OA}=3\underset{\sim}{i}-2\underset{\sim}{j}\), \(\overrightarrow{OB}=-\underset{\sim}{i}+\underset{\sim}{j}\). Suppose \(P\) is a point on \(AB\) such that \(\overrightarrow{OP}\perp\overrightarrow{AB}\). Find \(\overrightarrow{OP}\).
questions.hint: Let \(P=(x,y)\). TWO conditions: (1) \(\overrightarrow{OP}\perp\overrightarrow{AB}\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{OP}\cdot\overrightarrow{AB}=0\); (2) \(P\) is ON line \(AB\), i.e. \(\overrightarrow{AP}\) is a multiple of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) (equal gradients). Solve the two equations together.

steps.explain: Perpendicular: dot product zero, with \(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}x\\ y\end{pmatrix}\).

\(P\) on line \(AB\): the line through \(B(-1,1)\) with direction \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\ 3\end{pmatrix}\) has gradient \(\dfrac{3}{-4}\). Gradient from \(P\) to \(B\): \(\dfrac{1-y}{-1-x}\). Set equal.
Solve: from (1) \(y=\dfrac{4x}{3}\). Substitute into (2): \(3x+\dfrac{16x}{3}-1=0\Rightarrow\dfrac{25x}{3}=1\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{3}{25}\).

So \(P\left(\dfrac{3}{25},\dfrac{4}{25}\right)\) and \(\overrightarrow{OP}=\dfrac{3}{25}\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{4}{25}\underset{\sim}{j}\) (it is the foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) to \(AB\)). Check (1): \(-\dfrac{12}{25}+\dfrac{12}{25}=0\) ✓; check (2): \(\dfrac{9}{25}+\dfrac{16}{25}-1=0\) ✓.

steps.explain: The projection of \(\mathbf u\) onto \(\mathbf v\) is the 'shadow' of \(\mathbf u\) on the line of \(\mathbf v\). Its length is \(|\mathbf u||\cos\theta|\le|\mathbf u|\), so A is always true.

B compares with the length of \(\mathbf v\), which has nothing to do with the shadow. Counterexample: \(\mathbf u=2\mathbf i+2\mathbf j\), \(\mathbf v=\mathbf i\).

questions.stem: Find the vector projection of \(\underset{\sim}{p}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\ -3\end{pmatrix}\) onto \(\underset{\sim}{q}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.hint: Vector projection of \(\underset{\sim}{p}\) onto \(\underset{\sim}{q}\) is \(\dfrac{\underset{\sim}{p}\cdot\underset{\sim}{q}}{\left|\underset{\sim}{q}\right|^{2}}\,\underset{\sim}{q}\) (NOT divided by \(|q|\) once).

steps.explain: Write the formula for the vector projection of \(p\) onto \(q\).
Calculate the dot product.
Calculate \(|q|^{2}\) (squared length, so no square root is needed).
Substitute the scalar \(\dfrac{-10}{5}=-2\) and multiply the vector \(q\).

Check: the projection must be parallel to \(q\). \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\ -4\end{pmatrix}=-2q\) is parallel; options C and D contain \(\sqrt{5}\) which come from dividing by \(|q|\) once instead of \(|q|^{2}\).
So the correct choice is option B.

keyPoints.note: Vector projection formula: (p dot q) divided by |q| squared, times q.
